acts.evidence: The bank at Dorestad is cut into plots 18 m wide, each with its dam, and large storehouses stand on the newest ground, about 750-830. St Martin's of Utrecht held bank plots there of its own, and nobody might lodge in its men's houses or seize their goods.
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18 and (port.faith != christian or not feast)
acts.gives: Only where the house has a store: a plot (flag unlock_plot_<port id>), a factor (unlock_factor_<port id>), rented room (act_store_rented here), or a host who is a fast friend. Moves goods between the hold and this port's store (a wanted saved thing: a second Hold kept by port; lots keep their days and go on spoiling). An hour; half with carriers. A factor sells from it and buys into it at the board's price while you are away, for a twentieth (guess).
acts.changes: Goods in a store burn with the town. In a famine the count may open a grain store by force and pay the king's price (805). Nothing is moved on Sunday or a feast at a Christian port.

words.offer: Put goods into your store here, or take them out.
words.done: The door is barred again. The tally is cut.
words.refused: You have no store in this place.

acts.source: Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md sections 2 and 4 (Hoogstraat; Oorkondenboek Sticht Utrecht no. 56); chronicle_793.json 805-12; Design/content/CHAINS.md (unlock_plot, unlock_factor)

acts.name: Rent store room
acts.what: A stranger with no house left his goods under a host's roof, and the host answered for them as he answered for the guest. It cost a little and it tied the two men together.
acts.evidence: In the law of Kent a man who keeps a stranger three nights in his own house answers for him (?). At Dorestad shippers paid a due read as payment for lodging and protection. That a host took a fee for storing goods is a fair guess from these, not a recorded fact (?).
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18 and (port.faith != christian or not feast) and standing >= stranger
acts.gives: Room for one hold-load (the Gislinge's 660 kg) for 30 days, kept by port. 2 d a load a month (guess). Then use store. The host makes a theft good if he is friendly or more; if he is cool there is one chance in ten a month that something is gone.
acts.changes: Dear at a fair and when ships are many: double. An abbey stores for a friend of the house for alms. Where you are mistrusted nobody takes your goods in.

words.offer: Pay a householder to keep your goods a month.
words.done: He shows you the corner and the bar on the door.
words.refused: Nobody will take a stranger's goods in today.

acts.source: Hlothhere and Eadric 15 (from memory, by way of encounters/npc_roles_793.json, host) (?); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md section 4 ('giscot')

acts.name: Buy a plot
acts.what: The ground of a trading place was the king's or a bishop's, cut into narrow plots running to the water, and a merchant held his plot of that lord for a yearly due. With it came the right to land goods on his own strip.
acts.evidence: In 889 King Alfred and Ealdorman Æthelred gave the bishop of Worcester a plot in London with its own weights and measures for buying and selling; about 899 two plots at Æthelred's hythe, each with the right to moor ships along its width (?). Dorestad's bank is cut into plots 18 m wide, each with its own dam.
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18 and (port.faith != christian or not feast) and standing >= known
acts.gives: A house plot on the waterfront, held of the lord of the port. Price and what must be true: the port's entry unlock_plot_<port id> in story/unlocks_793.json (Dorestad 400 d, Lundenwic 500 d, Ripa 200 d); for a port with no entry, 100 d for each step of its size (ports_793.json size 1-5: guess). And 12 d a year at Martinmas (guess). Sets flag unlock_plot_<port id>. It gives a store of four hold-loads, a bed (lodge for nothing), leave to winter here, a berth of your own, and it is the first need of a factor and of works of your own. An heir has it after you. Lost if the due is three years unpaid, or with the port.
acts.changes: The grant is the lord's: ask an audience first, and bring a gift. Dorestad's plots end with Dorestad (863). London within the walls only from 886. Norse and Baltic markets: from the king's man of the market, for a gift. A monastery sells no ground. Nobody sells land to a stranger, and a great port asks more: Lundenwic wants you well regarded.

words.offer: Ask for a plot on the bank, to hold of the lord here.
words.done: The bounds are walked, and the neighbours saw it.
words.refused: No ground here is given to a man they hardly know.

acts.source: The London charters of 889 and 898/9 (Sawyer 346 and 1628), from memory (?); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md section 2; Design/content/CHAINS.md (unlock_plot)

acts.name: Lodge ashore
acts.what: A crew ashore slept in a householder's hall, in a monastery's guest house, or under their own sail on the strand. A host who kept a stranger answered for him, and one who shut his door was remembered for it.
acts.evidence: The Rule of St Benedict c. 53: guests are received as Christ, in a house of their own with a brother to see to them. The general capitulary of 802 forbids anyone to refuse a traveller roof, hearth and water (?). Alcuin's verses name Hrotberct of Dorestad, the greedy merchant who gives no lodging; Catla stayed there in a lodging-house about 850.
acts.when: moored
acts.gives: Ends the day: the clock runs to first light, as Rest does. The crew sleep dry: better than a night aboard (voyage_rules.json recover_in_port). One talk comes back at dawn. The host says who else has passed (one fact of the harbour, free). Three nights with one host: his feeling +3, and he will swear with you once.
acts.changes: At an abbey the bed is free and alms are looked for; in Lent no meat at the guest table. At a hall you are the lord's guest: a gift first. At a landing you sleep under the sail unless a farmer takes you in. In winter lodging is by the month (the winter screen): 20 d for four men, nothing on your own plot. A shunned man finds no host.

words.offer: Sleep ashore tonight, under a roof.
words.done: First light. The men slept dry.
words.refused: No door here opens to you. You sleep aboard.

acts.source: Rule of St Benedict c. 53; Capitulare missorum generale 802 c. 27 (from memory) (?); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md sections 2-3 (Alcuin, Carmen 4; Rimbert c. 20); Hávamál 2-4 (Bellows 1923)

acts.name: See the leech
acts.what: The sick were tended in a monastery's sick-house, or by a leech who let blood, set bones and gave herbs. What he knew was in his head and, by 900, in English books.
acts.evidence: The Rule of St Benedict c. 36 gives the sick a room apart and a brother to serve them. Bald's Leechbook is an English book of cures of the 9th to 10th century. Bede tells how Bishop John rebuked a house where a nun had been bled on the fourth day of the moon, when the moon and the tide are both growing (Historia ecclesiastica V.3).
acts.when: moored and health < 1
acts.gives: The crew's health up by a fifth now. A badly hurt man may be left with the leech (men -1): he is whole and waiting when you call again within 60 days, and gone home after. At an abbey no fee is asked and alms are looked for.
acts.changes: No blood is let while the moon is growing: with a new moon the leech gives herbs only and helps half as much (needs the moon's age from the sky). At a heathen port a woman who knows herbs does it, and a priest who hears thinks worse of you. In a plague year the abbey's gate is shut.

words.offer: Have the sick men seen to.
words.done: He binds it, gives a bitter drink, and says to rest.
words.refused: Your men are well. He sends you away.

acts.source: Rule of St Benedict c. 36; Bede, Historia ecclesiastica V.3; encounters/npc_roles_793.json (leech, wise_woman)

acts.name: Buy stores
acts.what: A crew ate bread, cheese, dried or salted fish and salt pork and drank ale and water, bought where she lay before each leg. Water was had for nothing at any well or river.
acts.evidence: Frankfurt (794) fixed bread: twelve wheat loaves of two pounds for a penny, and more loaves of rye, barley or oats. About 650 wells at Dorestad are lined with old Rhenish wine casks. In the famine years the king forbade selling grain dear or out of the realm (805, 806).
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18
acts.gives: Fills the ship's stores to the days asked for (the day stick shows the days the course needs): food goods and ale at this market's prices, into the hold (Voyage: 0.7 kg of food and 3 litres of drink a man a day; voyage_rules.json rations), and the water casks for nothing. Shown as 'days aboard'. In a plain year about a penny a day feeds four men. One hour to fetch and stow.
acts.changes: March to June grain is dear; in the famine of 793-794 bread costs three times as much and may not be sold out of the district. In Lent stores are fish, bread and ale. Food may be carted even on a Sunday (one of the three cartings the law allows): stores can be had then at an abbey's gate or a farm, though the market is shut. A northern port in winter sells dried fish and little else.

words.offer: Buy bread, fish and ale for the days ahead.
words.done: Stowed. So many days aboard.
words.refused: There is no food to be had here at this hour.

acts.source: Synod of Frankfurt 794 c. 4 (goods_793.json src frankfurt794; Design/economy_and_trade.md 1.2); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md section 2 (the wells); chronicle_793.json 805-12 and 806-03; voyage_rules.json; Admonitio generalis 789 c. 81

acts.name: Buy from makers
acts.what: Salt was cheapest at the pans, fish at the boats, querns where they were cut, cloth at the weaving house. Kings tried to drive such buying into their ports, where it could be seen and taxed.
acts.evidence: Edward the Elder: 'that no man buy out of port'; Athelstan: 'no man buy any property out of port over twenty pence; but let him buy there within': laws against what men were doing. Dorestad's workshops made combs, amber beads, querns, iron and cloth (2,889 loom weights) on the spot.
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18 and (port.faith != christian or not feast)
acts.gives: Opens a small market of only what this site makes (by its kind and the port's 'made' goods in goods_793.json: salt at a saltern, querns at a quarry, fish at a fishery, grain, cheese and wool at a field, combs, beads, pots or cloth at a workshop, iron at a smithy), at the market's cheap price (trade_rules.json market.cheap 0.85) with no gap between asking and paying, and a fifth of the market's stock. No toll is taken there and nobody witnesses it: the goods are unwitnessed, and in a toll port the toll man counts it as dodging if he learns (wanted deed: cheated_toll). Two hours out and back.
acts.changes: The season is everything: herring from September to November, salt in the dry months, grain after the harvest, wool at the June shearing. In English ports after about 930 not over 20 d worth. On Sunday or a feast at a Christian port nobody is working. At a landing this is the only way to buy.

words.offer: Go to where it is made and buy it there.
words.done: Bought at the maker's own price. Nobody saw it but you two.
words.refused: Nobody is at work there today.

acts.source: I Edward 1 and II Athelstan 12 (Thatcher 1907, checked at sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/560-975dooms.asp); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md section 2; seasons_793.json; trade_rules.json market

acts.name: Cross over
acts.what: A river town had its church on one bank and its market on the other, and a ferryman with a logboat between. Where two waters came near, carts took the goods over the neck of land.
acts.evidence: The capitularies allow a toll only where it is old and just, and none where no bridge or ferry helps the traveller (805, 809). Royal toll charters name the dues: on the bank, the bridge, the wheel and the gate. Goods for Hedeby crossed under 15 km of land from the Treene to the Schlei.
acts.when: moored and hour >= 5 and hour < 21
acts.gives: Takes the merchant, not the ship, to the sites the place file sets over the water, for this call. A ferry: a penny and an hour there and back. A ford: nothing, at low water only (TideModel). A bridge: nothing, unless an old toll stands on it. A portage: the cargo goes over in a day at 2 d a cart-load of about 500 kg, the boat herself on rollers in two days with carriers hired (guesses). The ferryman sees everyone who passes: asking him is a talk.
acts.changes: On ice it is walked for nothing, and carts cross: in the winter of 821-822 they crossed the Rhine, the Danube, the Elbe and the Seine for thirty days. In flood or a gale no ferry runs. At night the ferryman sleeps and a ford is not tried. On Sunday he carries people to Mass for nothing and no goods.

words.offer: Cross to the other side.
words.done: The far bank. The ferryman waits for his penny.
words.refused: Nobody is crossing now.

acts.source: chronicle_793.json 805, 809 and 821-winter-rivers-frozen (Design/economy_and_trade.md 1.3-1.4); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedeby (the portage); encounters/npc_roles_793.json (ferryman, carter)

acts.name: Fund a work
acts.what: Rich men of a place paid for what it needed: a church, a bridge, a well, a causeway. It was for the soul or for the name, and usually for both.
acts.evidence: Herigar, prefect of Birka, 'built a church on his own ancestral property' soon after 830. Swedish rune stones of the 11th century tell of bridges and causeways made for a kinsman's soul, as Jarlabanke's at Täby (?). Dorestad's wells were lined with merchants' wine casks.
acts.when: moored and hour >= 6 and hour < 18 and standing >= known
acts.gives: Lists this port's 'works' (the place file) whose years hold and whose 'needs' are met; the kinds of work are story/works_793.json. Paying a work's cost_d starts it; after its days it is done: flag unlock_work_<port id>_<what>, the town changes as the work's 'gives' says, and standing rises (wanted deed: funded_work, about cost_d / 100). It may be paid in parts over several calls (a saved sum). A work of the Church moves the priest and the bishop; a work of the port, the keeper and the merchants.
acts.changes: A stranger's silver is not wanted: be known here first. A work of the Church may be paid on a Sunday or feast, and is then seen by everyone. A work is lost with the town if it burns, but the name of it is kept. An heir is greeted by it.

words.offer: Ask what the place needs built.
words.done: The silver is counted out. The work will have your name on it.
words.refused: They take no gifts of that kind from a stranger.

acts.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 11 (Robinson 1921, checked at sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anskar.asp); the bridge stones (Upplands runinskrifter 127, 164, 212, 261) from memory (?); Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md section 2; Design/content/BRIEF_2.md (works)
